Phase 1 · Analyzer
1

Is this image a good hiding place?

Before anything is hidden, the system checks whether the cover is busy enough. A smooth sky or a plain wall would reveal the tiny changes embedding makes, so only images with rich texture are accepted. Texture is measured with Shannon entropy on the grayscale image: a flat picture scores near 0, a detailed one approaches the maximum of 8.

The brightness histogram of this cover. Pixel values are spread across the whole range, which is what makes the entropy high. Entropy = 7.6447, above the 7.6 threshold.
7.6447Shannon entropy
≥ 7.6suitability threshold
Highly Complextexture tier
α = 65embedding strength chosen
The entropy does double duty: it passes the image, and it sets the embedding strength α. A busier image can safely take stronger embedding.
Phase 2 · Payload protection
2

Lock the message and make it self-healing

The secret text is never hidden as plain words. First it is encrypted with AES-256, so only the holder of the password can read it. A random starting value (the IV) is attached so the same message never looks the same twice. Then a Reed-Solomon code adds 30% parity, which later lets the receiver repair byte errors the channel introduces.

The 56-character message after encryption + error coding (104 bytes)
25 18 63 9F 38 0E EA 87 14 C6 13 B5 86 FA 60 E7 25 18 63 9F 38 0E EA 87 14 C6 13 B5 86 FA 60 E7 ...
AES-256CBC encryption
+30%Reed-Solomon parity
104protected bytes
832bits to embed
The amber bytes are the IV; the rest is ciphertext plus parity. From here on the pipeline only moves bits, it never sees the original words.
Phase 3 · DWT-SVD embedding
3

Hide the bits in the image's structure

This is the heart of the method. The image's brightness is passed through a Haar wavelet transform, which separates it into frequency bands. We embed in the mid-frequency LH band, because it survives JPEG yet stays invisible. The LH band is exactly the edges and texture of the scene:

The LH sub-band of the cover. Bright lines are edges and detail; the flat sky is dark. The message is written into these coefficients, where it blends with natural detail.

Each 4×4 block of that band is factorised with SVD, and one bit is stored in the largest singular value using Quantization Index Modulation. Every bit is repeated 7 times and scattered, so no single patch of damage can erase it. The result looks identical to the original, drag the handle to compare:

coverstego (hidden data)
⇄

They are indistinguishable to the eye. But if we subtract the two and amplify the difference 25×, the hidden payload appears, sitting precisely on the textured regions:

Cover minus stego, amplified 25×. The bright points are the embedded bits. They cluster on edges and texture, never on smooth areas where they would be seen.

Phase 4 · The lossy channel
4

Send it through a hostile channel

A messaging platform does not forward your image untouched. It re-compresses it to save bandwidth. We simulate that with a JPEG attack at quality factor 50, the same punishing re-encoding WhatsApp or Facebook would apply.

The stego image after JPEG QF=50. This is what actually arrives at the receiver, degraded by compression.
survives
DWT-SVD (ours)
Singular values barely move under JPEG, so the hidden bit stays readable.
erased
Spatial LSB (classic)
JPEG removes the high-frequency noise that LSB hides in, so the message is lost.
Phase 5 · Blind recovery
5

Rebuild the message from the wreckage

The receiver needs only the image and the password, nothing else. It reads a tiny self-describing header, pulls the bits back out of the singular values, and repairs them in two layers: a majority vote across the 7 scattered copies of each bit, then Reed-Solomon to fix whatever errors remain. Finally AES-256 decrypts the result.

Every figure on this page was produced by running the actual pipeline on cover image 0009.png (2040 x 1524 px): entropy filter, AES-256 + Reed-Solomon, DWT-SVD embedding, a JPEG QF=50 attack, and blind extraction. PSNR 39.36 dB, SSIM 0.9628, raw BER 0.12%.
